A folded elephant trunk in a small-calibre true lumen during surgery for chronic aortic dissection should be avoided due to the risk of haemolysis. This is because inserting such a large and rigid foreign body into a narrow lumen can cause trauma to the blood vessels and lead to haemolytic anaemia, a condition characterized by excessive destruction of red blood cells.

In contrast, attempting to insert an elephant trunk in a small-calibre true lumen during surgery for chronic aortic dissection is likely not beneficial. Instead, surgeons may advocate for complete replacement of the dissected parts of the aorta if it is technically possible and safe to do so.

It's essential to note that the severity of TAI (truncus arteriosus) injury can be influenced by the sharpness of the aortic arch, with an inverse relationship between severity and aortic arch index.
